body:
### What would you like to be added?

Based on recent experiments with API server write throughput, we propose a multi-pronged effort to address severe allocation bottlenecks.

**1. Optimize the "Happy Path"**
* **Reduce PATCH Allocations:** Significantly reduce allocations for the PATCH path . Specifically, target `managedFields` patching and SSA tracking, which currently account for over half of allocations. Tracked in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/142228
* **Storage Bytes Passthrough**: Provide safeguards allowing us to safely pass through objects serialized in etcd to clients. Tracked as part of KEP https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/6407

**2. Optimize the "Bad Path" (Degraded States)**
* **Resilient Watch Propagation:** Implement https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/6268 to prevent watch breaking due to temporary CPU/network blips by allowing unsynchronized watchers to reread from cached objects.
* **Direct Watch Cache Reads for Informers:** Replace API server admission informers with Listers that read directly from the watch cache. This removes a heavy source of allocations while halving the memory needed by the API server. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/142304
* **Serve All Gets from Cache:** Ensure all Gets are served from the cache (including Gets triggered by TXN conflicts). This makes load on etcd and allocations much more predictable by removing a costly fallback. Tracked as part of KEP https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/6407

While most of these improvements are optimizations, "Serve all Gets from cache" may require a KEP update. The main risk is lock contention; however, thanks to the major rewrites of the watch cache in 1.37, we have removed almost all copying from under the lock and now rely on immutable btree snapshots to efficiently scale reads. 

Would like to get feedback on what is KEP worthy.

Implementing all those improvements allowed us reduce the allocation factor of API server from 100-180x to stable 50x and achieve over 4k QPS stable QPS on 30KB pods using single c4-standard-144 machine running kind cluster. Around that point we stopped seeing improvements from reducing allocations. Next stop: watch cache.

### Why is this needed?


Following the SIG Scalability proposals to introduce Resource Size as a new dimension (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/134375) and establish a realistic "Pod Shape" (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/138415), we have updated the list benchmark https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-scalability-benchmarks#gce-benchmark-list and introduced new write throughput benchmarks https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-scalability-benchmarks#gce-benchmark-write-throughput using this new pod shape. 

While investigating the bottlenecks in the write throughput benchmark (with help from @Jefftree), we identified the primary limiting factor: **Allocations**. 

#### 1. The Allocation Ceiling
**The API server allocates over 1MB of memory to apply a trivial patch on a 10KB pod object. This is a >100x allocation factor on the *happy path*** (which includes storing it in etcd, observing on watch, storing in the watch cache, and propagating to 10-20 watchers).

During our investigation, we discovered that the Go runtime hits a hard ceiling around 6GB/s of memory allocations on a `c4-highmem-144` machine. At this ceiling, CAS operations during the GC sweep phase start burning >50% of the CPU, fully saturating the node. We are in contact with the Go team to reproduce this behavior. In the meantime, tuning the garbage collector (`GOGC=400`) provided some relief, allowing us to hit allocation rates above 11GB/s, but a fundamental fix in the API server is still necessary.

#### 2. Sticky Degradation on Disruptions
The >100x allocation factor only accounts for the happy path. On any short disruption (e.g., watch breaks, transaction conflicts), the API server enters a degraded state:
* Watch breaking prevents the watch cache serialization cache from working
* Built into API server admission policy informer can quickly start relisting
* Conflicting TXNs cause the API server to fetch objects directly from etcd and decode them

In each these scenarios, **allocations easily double, turning a short disruption into a persistent, sticky degradation.** 

Hitting this allocation ceiling causes a sticky degradation that requires lowering the throughput by a factor of 2x-3x before the API server can recover. Consequently, improving QPS is only sustainable if the increase is gradual (<10% at a time) and at a steady state. Any burst immediately pushes the API server into a degraded state. 

Only by systematically addressing these degradation factors can we achieve a robust state where the API server can instantly jump to max QPS and reliably recover from bursts.

/sig scalability 
/sig api-machinery
/cc @Jefftree @p0lyn0mial @wojtek-t @liggitt

hey @serathius 
I was thinking of starting with the PATCH allocation part, especially around managedFields patching / SSA tracking, since this seems like a relatively focused area and is identified as a major source of allocations. Before I start digging into the implementation, I wanted to check whether you or someone else is already actively working on this part, and whether you would recommend this as a good piece to take up.

One measurement gap here seems worth pinning down before optimizing the individual degraded-state paths: recovery dynamics after a burst.

The issue notes that:

- a short disruption can push allocations much higher,
- recovery may require dropping throughput by 2-3x, and
- a gradual ramp can remain stable where a sudden jump to the same QPS does not.

That means steady-state max QPS alone may not characterize the system very well.

Would it make sense to add an A/B/A-style scalability experiment?

For example:

A1: run at ~60-70% of known sustainable write QPS until stable
B: briefly burst above the allocation ceiling
A2: return to exactly the same QPS as A1

Then compare A1 vs A2 and record something like:

- time to return within 10% of the pre-burst allocation/latency baseline
- peak allocation amplification
- excess-allocation or excess-latency area under the curve during recovery
- GC CPU / frequency
- APF queueing and any relist / watch-break / txn-conflict signals

If A1 and A2 differ materially under identical input load, that gives us a direct measure of the hysteresis described here.

This also seems like it could provide a common evaluation surface for #142228 and the degraded-state fixes listed above, rather than giving each optimization its own success metric. If the experiment becomes useful, kubernetes/perf-tests#4205 also looks like a natural place to make the resulting cross-run recovery data easier to compare.

ClusterLoader2 already has phased/stepped load primitives, so if this direction is useful I'd be interested in starting with the smallest experimental perf-tests scenario rather than changing production code first.

Thanks a lot for writing that down. I'm overall supportive except from potentially this point:

> Direct Watch Cache Reads for Informers: Replace API server admission informers with Listers that read directly from the watch cache. This removes a heavy source of allocations while halving the memory needed by the API server.

This has a potential to mess up what is currently clearly layered in kube-apiserver.
I acknowledge the potential impact from it, but I think we should first loop at the POC to make a decision if it will not make the system visibly more error-prone and harder to maintain.

@liggitt - for your thoughts on ^^

> This has a potential to mess up what is currently clearly layered in kube-apiserver.
I acknowledge the potential impact from it, but I think we should first loop at the POC to make a decision if it will not make the system visibly more error-prone and harder to maintain.

Definitely, let me create a PoC.
Discussed it with @liggitt and @wojtek-t. There are part of this proposal that we would like to track so I will create a umbrella KEP for that.
Prepared the PoC that implements pod lister interface by directly calling watch cache in transparent way for admission. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/142304

For allocations improvement we are a little blocked with the problem of watch breaking. https://perf-dash.k8s.io/#/?jobname=benchmark%20write%20throughput&metriccategoryname=GenericMeasurements&metricname=WatchTerminationRate&resource=pods

We need to land https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/6268 to be able to measure the other improvements. Or we would need adjust the test to remove terminations.
